title: SQL vs NoSQL Decision Framework
description: Apply a structured framework to choose between SQL and NoSQL databases for your C# application, based on data shape, consistency needs, and scale requirements.

data.text: The SQL versus NoSQL debate is often presented as a binary choice, but it is really a question of data shape and access patterns. SQL databases excel at structured, relational data with strong consistency guarantees. NoSQL databases excel at flexible schemas, horizontal scaling, and specific access patterns like key-value lookups or document queries. The senior engineer evaluates the actual data and how it will be used, not the marketing of either camp.

In a C# application, SQL databases pair naturally with EF Core, Dapper, and LINQ. NoSQL databases pair with specialized client libraries, document mappers, and eventual consistency patterns. Both can be the right choice, and many modern applications use both: SQL for transactional data and NoSQL for caching, session state, or content management.

data.title: When SQL is the right choice
items: Data has clear relationships: orders belong to customers, products belong to categories.
Strong consistency is required: financial transactions, inventory counts, audit logs.
The schema is stable and well-understood.
Complex queries with joins, aggregations, and reporting are common.
ACID transactions across multiple entities are needed.

data.title: When NoSQL is the right choice
items: Data is naturally document-oriented: JSON configurations, content, user profiles.
Schema flexibility is important: the data shape evolves frequently.
Horizontal scaling across many nodes is a hard requirement.
Write throughput is extremely high and reads are simple key-value or range queries.
Eventual consistency is acceptable for the use case.

data.title: Polyglot persistence is normal
data.text: Modern applications rarely choose one database for everything. A typical C# application might use PostgreSQL for orders and customers, Redis for session cache, and MongoDB for product catalog content. Choosing the right database per bounded context is senior-level thinking; choosing one database for the whole system is not.

data.title: SQL vs NoSQL evaluation steps
items: Map the data entities and their relationships. Are they naturally relational?
Identify consistency requirements: can the application tolerate eventual consistency?
Estimate read and write throughput at peak load. Does either exceed a single SQL server's capacity?
Consider schema evolution: how often does the data shape change, and how painful are migrations?
Evaluate operational complexity: does the team have expertise in the chosen NoSQL database?
Check ecosystem support: are there mature .NET client libraries and migration tools?

data.title: Database selection pitfalls
items: Choosing NoSQL because it is trendy, without analyzing data relationships or consistency needs.
Using SQL for highly unstructured, schema-less data that changes every sprint.
Forgetting that NoSQL does not eliminate the need for data modeling; it just changes the modeling approach.
Ignoring query patterns: a database that cannot serve your common queries efficiently is the wrong database regardless of its theoretical scalability.

data.title: Choose a database for three data domains
data.description: Apply the SQL vs NoSQL framework to realistic data domains.
steps: Consider three data domains: user accounts and authentication, product catalog, and session/analytics events.
For each domain, identify the data shape, consistency requirements, and access patterns.
Recommend SQL or NoSQL for each domain with a written rationale.
For at least one domain, explain why the opposite choice would be problematic.
Consider whether a hybrid approach (SQL for one domain, NoSQL for another) makes sense.
data.expectedOutcome: A database selection recommendation for each domain with a written rationale using the decision framework.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: SQL is better for structured, relational data with strong consistency requirements.
NoSQL is better for flexible schemas, high write throughput, and horizontal scaling.
Polyglot persistence is normal; use the right database per bounded context.
Evaluate data shape, consistency, throughput, and team expertise before choosing.
data.takeaway: The database is the foundation of your application's data story. Senior engineers choose the storage model that matches the data's natural shape and the application's actual access patterns.
